tool.name: Google Cloud
tool.tagline: Google's public cloud for compute, data, networking and AI
tool.description: Google Cloud is Google's public cloud platform: virtual machines, serverless containers, Kubernetes, managed databases, BigQuery analytics and Vertex AI, all on Google's global network and managed through one resource hierarchy and IAM model. Learning it lets you deploy, secure and run production systems on infrastructure used by many of the world's largest workloads.

glossary.def: A large building full of servers, with its own power, cooling and network links, where cloud providers run their machines.
A cloud service where the provider runs, patches and repairs the machines underneath, so you only use the service itself.
Data leaving a region or a cloud provider's network, for example to users on the internet. Cloud providers usually charge for it by the gigabyte.
A way of writing a range of IP addresses, like 10.10.0.0/20: the number after the slash says how many leading bits are fixed. A smaller number means a bigger range.
A virtual private network: an encrypted tunnel across the internet that joins two private networks, such as an office network and a cloud network, as if they were one.
Sending a small share of real traffic to a new version first, so problems show up for few users before everyone gets it.
An address only reachable from inside a private network, such as a VPC network, and not from the internet.
A public address that computers anywhere on the internet can use to reach a machine.
In Google Cloud: settings and access granted on an organization or folder automatically apply to every folder, project and resource beneath it.
In gcloud: one saved setting, such as the default project or region, kept in a configuration.
In Cloud Storage: one stored file, made of its bytes plus metadata such as its name, size and type.
Deciding which path network traffic takes to reach an address. In Google Cloud, a VPC network's routes say where traffic for each address range goes next.
Limits set in advance that stop people from making unsafe changes, such as an organization policy that forbids public buckets.
A geographic area where Google Cloud has data centers, such as europe-west1 in Belgium. Each region contains several zones.
One separate site inside a region, with its own power, cooling and network, so a failure in one zone doesn't affect the others.
A storage location that keeps copies of your data in several regions at once, such as US or EU.
The Google Cloud website (console.cloud.google.com) where you can see and change everything by clicking.
A free Linux machine Google runs for you, opened as a terminal in your browser, already signed in and with gcloud and other tools installed.
Google Cloud's tree of organization, folders and projects. Every resource sits in one project, and settings granted higher up apply below.
The permanent, globally unique name of a Google Cloud project, such as shop-prod-4821, used in commands. The project number is a second permanent ID Google assigns.
A rule set on the organization, a folder or a project that limits what can be configured below it, such as which regions may be used.
Google Cloud's command-line tool: almost anything you can click in the console can be typed as a gcloud command.
A named set of gcloud settings, such as which account, project and region to use, so you can switch between them with one command.
The Google Cloud account that holds how you pay and receives the charges for the projects linked to it.
Small monthly allowances of some Google Cloud services that never expire, such as one tiny VM and a few gigabytes of storage.
Anyone or anything that can be given access in IAM: a user, a group, a service account, a whole domain, or everyone (allUsers).
A named bundle of permissions, such as roles/storage.objectViewer (read files in Cloud Storage), that you grant to principals.
The list of IAM bindings attached to a resource, saying which principals get which roles there.
One entry in an allow policy: a role together with the principals who are given it.
A small service built into every Google Cloud VM and runtime that tells code about its environment and hands out short-lived tokens for the attached service account.
A service account that a Google service uses behind the scenes to act in your project, such as Cloud Build reading your files.
A downloadable JSON file that works like a permanent password for a service account. It leaks easily, so attached service accounts are preferred.
The size of a Compute Engine VM: how many CPUs and how much memory it has, named like e2-medium (family plus size).
A name such as debian-12 that always points to the newest version of an operating-system image, so new VMs get the latest patches.
A network-attached disk for Compute Engine VMs that keeps its data when the VM stops and can outlive the VM.
A Google service that checks who you are before letting you reach an app or a VM, so you can SSH into VMs that have no public address.
A shell script stored in a VM's settings that runs every time the VM starts, used for simple setup.
A much cheaper Compute Engine VM made from spare capacity, which Google can stop at any moment with 30 seconds' warning.
A regional slice of a VPC network that owns one range of IP addresses; VMs get their internal addresses from it.
The two firewall rules every VPC network has at the lowest priority: deny all incoming traffic and allow all outgoing traffic.
A text label, such as http-server, put on a VM so firewall rules and routes can pick which VMs they apply to.
A named top-level container for files (objects) in Cloud Storage, with a fixed location and a name unique across Google Cloud.
An optional Cloud Storage bucket setting that gives real folders, instead of folders that are only parts of object names.
A Cloud Storage setting that makes IAM the only thing deciding access to a bucket, switching off old per-object permission lists.
A link to one Cloud Storage object that works without signing in until a built-in expiry time, used to share a file safely.
Keeping deleted data for a while (7 days by default in Cloud Storage) so it can be restored if it was deleted by mistake.
In Cloud Run: an unchangeable snapshot of a service's image and settings, created by every deploy. Traffic can be split between revisions.
A Cloud Run container that runs a task to completion and then stops, instead of waiting for web requests.
Google Cloud's managed MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server databases: Google runs the database server, backups and updates for you.
Google Cloud's private storage for container images and software packages, organised into repositories inside a project.
Google Cloud's service that runs build steps (each in its own container) for you, such as building and pushing an image or deploying an app.

The fixed order in which Google's client libraries look for credentials: an environment variable, your gcloud login file, then the metadata server. The same code then works on a laptop and in production.
Acting as a service account using your own login: Google hands you short-lived tokens for it, after checking you hold the Token Creator role on it.
The project whose usage limits and billing an API call is counted against when you call with your personal login rather than a service account.
A saved description of a Compute Engine VM (machine type, image, disks, startup script) used to create many identical VMs. It cannot be edited once created.
A group of identical VMs created from one instance template, which Google keeps at the wanted size, repairs, scales and updates for you.
A managed instance group feature: a VM that fails its health check is deleted and recreated automatically.
Replacing the VMs or containers of a group a few at a time with a new version, so the service keeps running during the change.
A Cloud Storage price tier chosen by how often data is read: Standard, Nearline, Coldline or Archive. Colder tiers store cheaper but charge to read and have minimum storage times.
A charge per gigabyte for reading data from the colder Cloud Storage classes (Nearline, Coldline, Archive).
The shortest time an object in a cold storage class is billed for, even if deleted earlier: 30, 90 or 365 days.
An automatic action on a bucket's objects when a condition is met, such as moving them to a colder storage class or deleting them after N days.
A bucket setting that keeps the previous copy of an object (a noncurrent version) when it is overwritten or deleted, so it can be restored.
A bucket rule that forbids deleting or replacing objects until they reach a given age; it can be locked so nobody can remove it.
Restoring a database to exactly how it was at any chosen moment, rebuilt from backups plus its log of changes.
A small program that runs next to your app and connects it to Cloud SQL, checking identity with IAM and encrypting traffic so you don't handle certificates.
A way to deploy a single function to Google Cloud: Google builds it into a container and runs it on Cloud Run when a web request or an event arrives.
A notice that something happened, such as a file finished uploading or a message arrived, which can start a function or workflow.
Google Cloud's service that delivers events from Google services and audit logs to Cloud Run services and functions.
An Artifact Registry setting that stops a tag such as v1.2.0 from ever being pointed at a different image once pushed.
One stage of a Cloud Build run: a container image plus arguments, which sees the same /workspace directory as the other steps.
A variable in a Cloud Build config filled in at build time, such as $PROJECT_ID or $SHORT_SHA; your own must start with an underscore.
A rule that starts a Cloud Build run automatically, usually when code is pushed to a Git repository or a pull request is opened.
Cloud Build machines connected to your own VPC network, so builds can reach private machines and databases.
A named channel in Pub/Sub that publishers send messages to.
A named reader of a Pub/Sub topic. Each subscription gets its own copy of every message; programs sharing one subscription share its messages.
Telling Pub/Sub that a message was handled, so it isn't delivered again. If no ack arrives within the ack deadline, the message is redelivered.
A topic where Pub/Sub moves a message after it has failed delivery a set number of times, so a broken message stops looping forever.
A database built for scanning and summarising huge tables (reports and analytics), rather than for an app's many small reads and writes.
Google Cloud's serverless data warehouse: you load tables and ask questions in SQL, and Google supplies the machines.
BigQuery's unit of computing power. On-demand queries borrow slots from a shared pool; capacity pricing reserves a number of them.
In BigQuery: a named group of tables with one location and its own access settings.
Running something in a 'show me what would happen' mode without doing it: a BigQuery dry run reports the bytes a query would read; a dry-run policy only logs violations.
A program installed on a Compute Engine VM that sends its logs and detailed metrics (memory, disk) to Cloud Logging and Monitoring.
Writing each log entry as named fields (one line of JSON) instead of free text, so you can search by field such as order_id=42.
A rule that sends log entries matching a filter to a destination: a log bucket, BigQuery, Cloud Storage or Pub/Sub.
A storage area for logs in Cloud Logging. _Required keeps audit logs 400 days for free; _Default keeps everything else 30 days.
A rule on a log sink that drops matching entries so they are never stored, cutting cost.
A number produced by counting (or measuring a value in) log entries that match a filter, which Cloud Monitoring can chart and alert on.
In a Cloud Monitoring query: the step that turns each series' raw points into one value per regular interval, such as a rate or an average per minute.
In a Cloud Monitoring query: the step that combines many time series into one, such as summing request counts across all instances.
A Cloud Monitoring rule: one or more conditions on metrics or logs, how long they must hold, and the notification channels (email, SMS, Slack, PagerDuty...) to tell.
A Cloud Monitoring test that regularly requests your site from several places in the world and can alert when it is down as seen from outside.
A service level objective: a target for how good your service must be, such as 99.9% of requests succeed over 28 days. Burn rate is how fast you are using up the allowed failures.
The share of requests allowed to fail under an SLO (0.1% for a 99.9% target). Spending it fast triggers alerts.
Google Cloud's service for storing passwords, API keys and other small secret values, with versions, per-secret access control and a record of reads.
One value of a secret in Secret Manager. Values are never edited: adding a new value creates a new version, and 'latest' points to the newest enabled one.
A Google Cloud load balancer that understands HTTP and HTTPS, so it can route by URL, add certificates, Cloud CDN and Cloud Armor.
A Google Cloud load balancer that only looks at addresses and ports, so it works for any TCP or UDP traffic; the passthrough kind keeps the visitor's real IP address.
Google Cloud's filter in front of a load balancer that blocks attacks and abusive traffic, such as floods of requests or known attack patterns.
The front of a Google Cloud load balancer: the IP address and port that visitors connect to, pointing at a proxy or backend.
The part of an Application Load Balancer that chooses a backend service by host name and path, e.g. /images/* to a bucket.
The load balancer resource that lists the backends traffic goes to, with the health check, timeouts and CDN settings.
A network endpoint group: a load-balancer backend that points at a Cloud Run service or function (serverless NEG), or at individual containers or VMs.
Announcing the same IP address from many places in the world, so each visitor is served by the nearest one.
Google's managed service that lets VMs without external IP addresses make outgoing connections to the internet through shared public addresses, while nothing can connect in.
A subnet setting that lets VMs without external IP addresses reach Google services such as Cloud Storage, without NAT.
A connection from your VPC network to a Google-managed network, so services like Cloud SQL get a private IP address in a range you reserve.
A way to reach a Google service or another team's service as one private IP address inside your VPC network, without joining the two networks' address ranges.
One VPC network owned by a host project and used by several service projects, so a central team manages the network while app teams own their projects.
Connecting two VPC networks so their machines can talk over private addresses. It is non-transitive: A peered with B and B with C doesn't connect A to C.
Every read returns the latest successfully written value, never an older copy.
Handling more load by adding more machines rather than a bigger machine.
Google's relational SQL database that spreads writes across many machines and regions while staying strongly consistent, for very large or global apps.
A database that stores JSON-like documents in collections instead of rows in fixed tables; each document can have its own set of fields.
Google Cloud's serverless document database, with live updates pushed to apps and offline support in its mobile and web libraries.
Google Cloud's NoSQL database for enormous volumes of data read and written by key, answering in a few milliseconds; used for sensor data, time series and ad systems.
The open-source system for running many containers across many machines: you describe what should run, and it starts, restarts and spreads the containers to match.
One machine (in GKE, a Compute Engine VM) in a Kubernetes cluster that runs containers.
The managing part of a Kubernetes cluster: it stores what should run, schedules containers onto nodes and answers kubectl commands.
The command-line tool for talking to a Kubernetes cluster: create, inspect and change what runs in it.
The smallest unit Kubernetes runs: one or more containers that start together on the same node and share an IP address.
A Kubernetes object that keeps a set number of identical Pods running and rolls out new versions gradually.
A Kubernetes object that gives a group of Pods one stable address and spreads traffic across them. Type LoadBalancer also gets an outside address.
The CPU and memory a Pod says it needs, which Kubernetes uses to place it and which Autopilot bills for.
Google Kubernetes Engine: Google Cloud's managed Kubernetes, which runs the control plane (and, in Autopilot mode, the nodes) for you.
The GKE mode where Google manages the nodes too; you deploy Pods and pay for the CPU, memory and storage they request.
A group of GKE nodes that share one machine type and settings; a Standard cluster can have several.
A GKE setting (Rapid, Regular, Stable or Extended) that decides how quickly Google upgrades your cluster to new Kubernetes versions.
GKE networking where Pods and Services get IP addresses from extra ranges on your subnet, so other machines in the VPC network can reach Pods directly.
The secret value used to scramble data and to unscramble it again. Anyone with the key can read the data; nobody else can.
Google Cloud's service for creating, storing, rotating and controlling encryption keys.
A named group of keys in Cloud KMS, in one location. It can never be deleted.
Regularly creating a new version of a key or secret. In Cloud KMS, old key versions stay usable for decrypting data they protected.
A hardware security module: a tamper-resistant device that holds encryption keys so they can never be copied out, even by administrators.
Encrypting data with a fresh local data key, then having Cloud KMS encrypt (wrap) that data key. The wrapped key is stored with the data.
Customer-managed encryption keys: telling a Google service to protect your data with a key you control in Cloud KMS, so you can revoke it.
The most common tool for infrastructure as code: you write what should exist in .tf files, 'plan' shows the difference from reality and 'apply' makes the changes.
Terraform's plug-in for one platform, such as the google provider for Google Cloud, which knows how to create each kind of resource.
Terraform's record of the resources it created and their current settings, used to work out what to change. It can contain secrets.
A reusable bundle of Terraform code that creates a group of resources, such as a whole VPC network with subnets.
Google's family of generative AI models that write text and code and understand images, available in Google Cloud through Vertex AI.
Google Cloud's platform for machine learning: generative models, training your own models, deploying them behind endpoints, and pipelines.
Vertex AI's catalogue of ready-to-use models from Google, partners and the open-source community.
Running a model over a large set of inputs at once, from files or tables, instead of answering one request at a time.
A Cloud Billing rule that sends alerts when spending (actual or forecast) reaches set fractions of an amount. It does not stop spending.
A key-value tag on a Google Cloud resource, such as team=checkout, used to group costs and resources.
A large discount in exchange for promising to use a certain amount of resources, or spend, for one or three years.
An automatic discount for some Compute Engine VM types that run for most of a month.
Google Cloud's advice service that points out waste (idle VMs, unattached disks, unused addresses) and unused permissions.
An IAM role you define with exactly the permissions you need, for when no predefined role fits.
A rule attached to an IAM binding, written in CEL, that limits when it applies: until a date, to resources with a name prefix, or to tagged resources.
Common Expression Language: a small language for writing true/false rules, such as request.time < timestamp('2026-12-31'), used in IAM Conditions and organization policies.
In Google Cloud: a key-value pair attached to a resource or project for use in IAM Conditions and organization policies (unlike a label, which is for grouping and costs).
An IAM policy that forbids chosen permissions to a set of principals, checked before allow policies, so no role can grant them.
Letting a program outside Google Cloud (or a Pod in GKE) swap the token its own platform gives it for short-lived Google credentials, so no key files are needed.
A CEL rule on a Workload Identity Federation provider that names which outside identities to trust, such as one GitHub repository.
One rule in the Organization Policy Service about how resources may be configured, such as allowed locations or no public buckets.
An organization policy rule you write yourself as a CEL condition on a resource's fields, for services that support it.
A Google Cloud feature that fences a set of projects so data in protected services can only move within the fence, even for callers with valid credentials.
The VPC Service Controls fence: a set of projects plus the restricted services whose data may not leave it.
A condition on a caller's IP range, device or identity under which it may reach a service perimeter from outside.
A VPC Service Controls exception allowing a named outside caller to reach services inside a perimeter.
A VPC Service Controls exception allowing a caller inside a perimeter to reach a named resource outside it.
Google Cloud's record of every API call on your resources: who did what, on which resource, when.
The audit log of changes to settings and configuration, such as creating a VM or changing an IAM policy. Always on and free.
The audit log of reads of configuration and reads or writes of your actual data. Off by default for most services because of its volume.
A log sink on an organization or folder that, with --include-children, routes the logs of every project beneath it, including future ones.
A security monitoring system that collects logs from many sources and watches them for signs of attack.
The service account Google creates for a log sink, which must be granted write access on the sink's destination.
An identity that exists only inside a Kubernetes cluster, which Pods run as. Workload Identity Federation can give it a Google Cloud identity too.
GKE nodes with no external IP addresses, so they can't be reached from the internet; they use Cloud NAT for outgoing traffic.
A Kubernetes rule saying which Pods may talk to which, used to block traffic between namespaces by default.
A GKE and Cloud Run control that only lets images run if your pipeline has signed or attested (vouched for) them.
A Kubernetes rule for how many Pods of an app may be down at once, so upgrades and maintenance never take them all.
An algorithm by which several copies of data agree on each change even if some copies fail, used by Spanner to keep replicas in step.
Google's clock API, backed by GPS and atomic clocks, that returns an interval guaranteed to contain the true time, which Spanner uses to order transactions.
The short pause Spanner takes before confirming a write, until its chosen timestamp is certainly in the past everywhere.
Spanner's guarantee that if one transaction finishes before another starts, every machine in the world sees them in that order.
One part of a database (one split or machine) getting most of the load while the rest sit idle, usually because new rows all have neighbouring keys.
Storing a child table's rows physically next to their parent row in Spanner, so reads and transactions on one parent stay on one split.
A Spanner read of data as of a moment slightly in the past (e.g. 10 seconds ago), which can be answered by the nearest copy without waiting.
In Spanner: one range of rows (by primary key) stored and replicated as a unit. Spanner divides and moves splits automatically.

concepts.name: Regions, zones and the service map
concepts.summary: How Google Cloud is laid out on the map (regions and zones) and how its many services group into families: compute, storage, networking and AI.
concepts.why: Everything you create lives in a place, and that choice decides how fast it answers your users, how well it survives outages, and what it costs.
concepts.body:
Google Cloud rents you computers, storage and ready-made software that run in Google's **data centers** — huge buildings full of servers. Each thing you create there, such as a VM or a place to keep files, is called a **resource**. Google looks after the machines underneath; that is what a **managed service** means.

Every service is controlled through an **API** (application programming interface): a fixed menu of operations one program can ask another to do, like "create a VM" or "list my files". Clicking in the website, typing a command and your own code all call the same API.

Before creating anything you need one idea: **location**. A **region** is a geographic area with its own group of data centers, named like `us-central1` (Iowa) or `europe-west1` (Belgium). Each region is split into three or more **zones**, such as `europe-west1-b`. Zones are separate sites with their own power and network links, so a fire or power cut in one shouldn't take down the others.

Some storage services also offer **multi-regions** (`US`, `EU`), which keep copies of your data in several regions at once.

Because of this, every resource covers a certain part of the map:
- **Zonal**: a VM and its disk live in one zone. If that zone has an outage, they are unavailable.
- **Regional**: a Cloud Run service (a way to run containers, covered later) is spread over all zones of its region, so it survives one zone failing.
- **Global**: some things, such as VM images and private networks, can be used from every region.

The services fall into rough families. **Compute** is places to run your programs: Compute Engine (VMs) and Cloud Run (containers). **Storage and databases** hold your data: Cloud Storage for files, and Cloud SQL for a **database** — a program that keeps organised data and lets you search it fast. **Networking** connects it all.

Two more families: **operations** — Logging and Monitoring, which collect your programs' messages and measurements so you can see what they are doing — and **AI**, software that learns from examples instead of following hand-written rules, offered through Vertex AI.

Pick a region close to your users that offers the services you need, and keep resources that talk to each other in one region. Traffic between regions is slower, and Google charges for it as **egress** — data leaving a region or leaving Google's network.
concepts.code:
# List regions and the zones of one region
gcloud compute regions list --format="value(name)" | head -5
# africa-south1
# asia-east1
# asia-east2
# ...
gcloud compute zones list --filter="region:europe-west1" --format="value(name)"
# europe-west1-b
# europe-west1-c
# europe-west1-d
takeaways: A region holds three or more separate zones
Resources are zonal, regional or global
Keep resources that talk to each other in one region to save time and egress charges
pitfalls: Running a single VM in one zone and expecting it to keep working when that zone has an outage.

quiz.q: Which of these lives in a single zone in Google Cloud?
options: A bucket in the EU multi-region
quiz.explain: A VM and its disk live in one zone; a Cloud Run service spans a region, VM images are global and a multi-region bucket spans several regions.

concepts.name: The console and Cloud Shell
concepts.summary: Find your way around the Google Cloud console website and use Cloud Shell, a free terminal in your browser with Google's tools ready to use.
concepts.why: It is the fastest way to start: nothing to install, you're already signed in, and the common tools are set up.
concepts.body:
The **Google Cloud console** (console.cloud.google.com) is the website where you click your way through Google Cloud. Everything you create lives inside a **project** — a named box for one app's resources (the next lessons explain projects properly). The project picker at the top of the page decides which project you are looking at, and most beginner confusion comes from being in the wrong one.

The navigation menu lists every product, and you can pin the ones you use. The search bar finds products, your own resources and documentation.

Click the terminal icon at the top to open **Cloud Shell**: a small Linux VM that Google starts for you, shown as a terminal inside your browser tab. It has `gcloud` (Google Cloud's command-line tool), `docker`, `kubectl`, `terraform`, Python, Node.js and Git preinstalled, and you're already signed in as yourself — no passwords or keys to set up.

Key facts:
- Your home directory (`$HOME`) sits on a 5 GB disk that is kept; everything outside it is reset each time Cloud Shell restarts.
- The selected project is stored in the environment variable `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT`.
- **Cloud Shell Editor** opens a code editor, similar to VS Code, on the same machine.
- Cloud Shell shuts down after about an hour without activity, and your home disk is deleted if you don't open Cloud Shell for 120 days.

Use the console to explore and learn what exists, and Cloud Shell or `gcloud` in a terminal to do things you can repeat exactly. Many console pages offer an "Equivalent command" button that shows the `gcloud` command doing the same as your clicks — a good way to learn the commands.
concepts.code:
# Inside Cloud Shell
echo $GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT        # shop-dev-4821
gcloud config list
# [core]
# account = you@example.com
# project = shop-dev-4821

gcloud projects list --format="table(projectId,name)"
df -h $HOME | tail -1             # ~5G persistent home disk
takeaways: Always check the project picker before changing anything
Cloud Shell comes signed in with the common tools installed
Only $HOME survives when Cloud Shell restarts
pitfalls: Installing tools system-wide (with `sudo apt install`) in Cloud Shell and expecting them to be there next time.

quiz.q: You installed a tool with apt in Cloud Shell yesterday and it is gone today. Why?
options: Only the home directory persists between sessions
Cloud Shell deletes tools after 24 hours
apt is blocked in Cloud Shell
quiz.explain: Cloud Shell's VM is recreated each time it starts; only the 5 GB home disk is kept.

concepts.name: Organization, folders and projects
concepts.summary: How Google Cloud organises everything: projects hold resources, folders group projects, an organization sits on top, and settings flow down.
concepts.why: Projects are where billing, usage limits and access are set, and rules set higher up apply to every project below.
concepts.body:
Think of a company's shared drive: files sit in folders, folders sit in bigger folders, and access you give on a folder covers everything inside it. Google Cloud arranges its resources the same way, in a tree called the **resource hierarchy**.

Every resource belongs to exactly one **project**. Projects can sit inside **folders**, and folders inside one **organization** — the top of the tree, which belongs to your company and is tied to its email domain (such as example.com).

A project has three identifiers:
- **Project ID**: chosen by you, unique across all of Google Cloud, and can never be changed (`shop-prod-4821`). Commands use this one.
- **Project number**: a number Google assigns, also permanent. It appears in the names of some accounts Google creates for you.
- **Name**: a display name you can change any time.

The project is the boundary for most settings: which services are switched on (each service's API must be enabled per project), **quotas** — usage limits such as how many CPUs you may run at once — which billing account pays, and most access grants. A common layout is one project per app per environment (`shop-dev`, `shop-prod`), grouped into folders such as `Production` and `Non-production`, or by team.

Two kinds of rules **inherit** down the tree: set them on a folder and they apply to every project inside. The first is access grants — who may do what, covered in the IAM lesson. The second is **organization policies**, limits such as "only use EU regions". A project can add access, but it can't remove access that was granted above it.

Personal accounts without an organization (a plain Gmail address) can still create projects; they just have no folders or organization-wide rules. Deleting a project shuts it down at once and deletes it for good after 30 days, during which you can still restore it.
concepts.code:
# Create a project inside a folder and make it the default
gcloud projects create shop-dev-4821 --name="Shop dev" --folder=123456789012
gcloud config set project shop-dev-4821

gcloud projects describe shop-dev-4821 --format="value(projectNumber,parent.type,parent.id)"
# 987654321098  folder  123456789012

# Walk up the tree
gcloud projects get-ancestors shop-dev-4821
# ID              TYPE
# shop-dev-4821   project
# 123456789012    folder
# 555555555555    organization
takeaways: Every resource lives in exactly one project
The project ID is unique and permanent; the name is just for display
Access grants and organization policies set on a folder or the organization apply to everything below
pitfalls: Putting dev and prod in one project, so one access grant or one quota affects both.

quiz.q: Someone is given read-only access on a folder. What can they see in a project inside that folder?
options: Nothing until access is granted on the project
Everything read-only access allows, inherited from the folder
quiz.explain: Access grants flow down the tree, so the folder grant applies to every project inside it.

concepts.name: The gcloud CLI
concepts.summary: Set up gcloud, switch between projects with named configurations, enable services, and shape output with --format and --filter.
concepts.why: gcloud is how you script, automate and reproduce everything you click in the console.
concepts.body:
The **gcloud CLI** is Google Cloud's command-line tool: almost anything you can click in the console you can also type as a `gcloud` command. It is installed together with `bq` (for BigQuery) and the older `gsutil`. Commands read like a sentence, `gcloud GROUP [SUBGROUP] ACTION`: `gcloud compute instances list` means "in Compute Engine, list the VMs".

Getting set up (Cloud Shell has already done this for you):
- `gcloud init` signs you in and picks a default project and region.
- `gcloud auth login` signs the CLI in as you, through your browser.
- `gcloud config set project ID` and `gcloud config set compute/region europe-west1` save defaults, so you can leave out `--project` and `--region` later.

These saved settings (gcloud calls them **properties**) live in a **configuration**. You can keep several named configurations — one per project or client, such as `dev` and `prod` — and switch with `gcloud config configurations activate prod`. For a single command, pass `--project` instead.

Each service must be **enabled** in a project before you can use it: `gcloud services enable run.googleapis.com` switches on Cloud Run's API. An error saying `SERVICE_DISABLED` or "API has not been used in project" means exactly this.

For scripts, every `list` or `describe` command accepts `--format` to choose the output shape (`json`, `yaml`, `table(...)`, or `value(...)` for bare values) and `--filter` to keep only matching items. `value()` prints just the value, perfect for saving into a shell variable.

Put `beta` or `alpha` after `gcloud` to reach preview features that aren't final yet, and add `--help` to any command for its full documentation.
concepts.code:
gcloud config configurations create dev
gcloud config set project shop-dev-4821
gcloud config set compute/region europe-west1
gcloud config configurations list          # IS_ACTIVE marks the current one

gcloud services enable run.googleapis.com artifactregistry.googleapis.com
gcloud services list --enabled --filter="name:run" --format="value(name)"
# run.googleapis.com

# Capture a value for scripting
PROJECT_NUMBER=$(gcloud projects describe shop-dev-4821 --format="value(projectNumber)")
echo $PROJECT_NUMBER                        # 987654321098
takeaways: Use named configurations to switch between projects safely
Enable a service's API before using it
--format=value(...) and --filter make gcloud easy to script
pitfalls: Running a destructive command against the wrong project because the active configuration was not the one you assumed.

quiz.q: A command fails with 'API has not been used in project ... or it is disabled'. What is the fix?
options: Ask for more access on the project
Enable the service with gcloud services enable
Switch to the beta command group
quiz.explain: Each service's API must be switched on per project before it can be used.

concepts.name: Billing accounts and the free tier
concepts.summary: How projects are linked to billing accounts, what the free trial and Free Tier cover, and what happens when billing is removed.
concepts.why: Nothing paid runs without a billing account, and understanding the link prevents surprise bills and surprise outages.
concepts.body:
A **Cloud Billing account** holds how you pay (a card or invoice details) and receives the charges. Each project is linked to at most one billing account, and one billing account usually pays for many projects. Paid services refuse to work in a project with no billing account linked.

Access to billing is separate from access to projects. People get **roles** — named bundles of permissions, explained in the IAM lesson — on the billing account itself: **Billing Account Administrator** manages the account, **Billing Account User** may link projects to it, and **Billing Account Viewer** can read costs. To link a project you need Billing Account User on the account *and* the right to change billing on the project (for example as the project's Owner).

New customers get a **free trial** credit (USD 300 to spend within 90 days, at the time of writing). Separately, the **Free Tier** gives small monthly allowances that never expire, such as one small `e2-micro` VM in certain US regions, a few GB of Cloud Storage in US regions, and free monthly amounts of Cloud Run and BigQuery.

If you **unlink billing** (or a script you set up does it automatically), paid resources are stopped and may be deleted. That is a blunt emergency switch, not a way to control costs. For day-to-day control you set **budgets** that send alerts, covered later.

Costs appear in the console's Billing reports within hours. For detailed analysis you can export them to BigQuery, Google's service for analysing large tables of data.
concepts.code:
gcloud billing accounts list
# ACCOUNT_ID            NAME              OPEN
# 01AB23-45CD67-89EF01  Main billing      True

gcloud billing projects link shop-dev-4821 --billing-account=01AB23-45CD67-89EF01
gcloud billing projects describe shop-dev-4821 --format="value(billingEnabled)"
# True
takeaways: One billing account pays for many projects; a project has at most one
Billing roles are granted on the billing account, not the project
Unlinking billing stops paid resources, so it is not a gentle cost control
pitfalls: Assuming a budget caps spending; a budget only sends alerts unless you automate an action.

quiz.q: What do you need to link a project to a billing account?
options: Only read access on the project
Billing Account User on the account plus billing rights on the project
Being an administrator of the organization
quiz.explain: Linking needs permission on both sides: use the billing account, and change billing on the project.

concepts.name: IAM: principals, roles and allow policies
concepts.summary: Who can do what: principals, basic vs predefined roles, and allow policies — and how grants on folders and projects add up.
concepts.why: IAM checks every action in Google Cloud; most access problems and many security incidents trace back to it.
concepts.body:
Every time anyone — a person, a script, a running app — asks Google Cloud to do something, Google first checks whether they're allowed. The system that decides is **Identity and Access Management (IAM)**. It answers one question: who can do what on which resource?

The "who" is a **principal**. Principals include a person (`user:ada@example.com`), a Google group (`group:devs@example.com`), a **service account** — an identity for a program rather than a person, covered next — a whole company domain (`domain:example.com`), and the special `allUsers`, meaning anyone on the internet.

The "what" is a **role**: a named bundle of **permissions**, where each permission is one action such as `storage.objects.get` (read a file in Cloud Storage). There are three kinds:
- **Basic** roles: Owner, Editor, Viewer. Broad and coarse; avoid them in production.
- **Predefined** roles: made by Google for each service, e.g. `roles/storage.objectViewer` or `roles/run.developer`. Use these by default.
- **Custom** roles: your own list of permissions, for when no predefined role fits.

The "which resource" part: you attach an **allow policy** to a resource — the organization, a folder, a project, or a single item such as one storage bucket. The policy is a list of **bindings**, each pairing one role with the principals who get it.

What someone may do on a resource is the sum of the bindings on it and on everything above it in the hierarchy. Grants only ever add access: to take access away, you remove the binding where it was made. (Google Cloud also has deny policies, an advanced feature.)

Good practice: grant roles to **groups**, not individuals; grant at the lowest level that works; and prefer predefined roles over Editor. `gcloud projects get-iam-policy` shows the bindings, and the console's Policy Troubleshooter explains why someone has or lacks a permission.
concepts.code:
# Let a group read objects in one bucket only
gcloud storage buckets add-iam-policy-binding gs://shop-dev-assets \
  --member="group:frontend@example.com" --role="roles/storage.objectViewer"

# Project-wide grant to a user
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding shop-dev-4821 \
  --member="user:ada@example.com" --role="roles/run.developer"

# Who has which role on the project?
gcloud projects get-iam-policy shop-dev-4821 \
  --flatten="bindings[].members" --format="table(bindings.role,bindings.members)"

# Which permissions are in a role?
gcloud iam roles describe roles/storage.objectViewer --format="value(includedPermissions)"
takeaways: A binding = one role + principals, attached to a resource
Prefer predefined roles over Owner/Editor/Viewer
Effective access is the sum of the resource's and all its ancestors' policies
Grant to groups at the lowest level that works
pitfalls: Granting Editor to make an error go away; it gives write access to nearly every service in the project.

quiz.q: Alice has roles/storage.admin on the project and no binding on bucket B. Can she delete objects in B?
options: Yes, the project grant is inherited by the bucket
No, bucket-level policies override project ones
Only if the bucket is public
quiz.explain: Allow policies are additive and inherited, so a project-level role applies to every bucket in it.

quiz.q: Which principal makes a resource readable by anyone on the internet?
quiz.explain: allUsers means any caller, authenticated or not.

concepts.name: Service accounts
concepts.summary: Identities for programs: create service accounts, attach them to whatever runs your code, and avoid long-lived key files.
concepts.why: Every VM, Cloud Run service and build acts as some service account, so giving each one only the access it needs starts here.
concepts.body:
A program that uses Google Cloud — say, an app that saves uploaded photos to Cloud Storage — needs an identity, just as you sign in with your Google account. A **service account** is that identity: an account for software, not a person. Its email looks like `app-sa@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com`. Like a user it receives IAM roles; unlike a user it has no password.

The safe way to use one is to **attach** it to the thing that runs your code: a VM, a Cloud Run service, a build. Code running there asks a small built-in service on the machine, the **metadata server**, for a **token** — a short-lived digital pass that proves "I am this service account" and expires within an hour. Nothing secret is ever saved to disk.

Two separate permission questions:
- What can the service account do? Grant roles **to** it (e.g. `roles/pubsub.publisher` on one message topic).
- Who may use it? To attach a service account to a resource you need `roles/iam.serviceAccountUser` **on** that service account. This stops someone who can deploy apps from borrowing a powerful identity.

Google also creates **default service accounts**, such as the Compute Engine default `PROJECT_NUMBER-compute@developer.gserviceaccount.com` that VMs use unless you choose another, and **service agents**, accounts Google's own services use behind the scenes. Prefer one dedicated service account per app with only the roles it needs — the principle of **least privilege**.

**Service account keys** are JSON files that work like a permanent password for the account. They leak easily (copied to laptops, committed to Git) and keep working until someone deletes them. Avoid them: inside Google Cloud attach service accounts; for people, use impersonation (acting as a service account with your own login); for programs outside Google Cloud, use Workload Identity Federation. Both come later. Many organizations block key creation entirely.
concepts.code:
PROJECT=shop-dev-4821
gcloud iam service-accounts create orders-api --display-name="Orders API"
SA=orders-api@$PROJECT.iam.gserviceaccount.com

# What the workload may do: publish to one topic
gcloud pubsub topics add-iam-policy-binding orders \
  --member="serviceAccount:$SA" --role="roles/pubsub.publisher"

# Who may deploy things that run as it
gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding $SA \
  --member="group:orders-devs@example.com" --role="roles/iam.serviceAccountUser"

# Attach it to a Cloud Run service
gcloud run deploy orders-api --image=us-docker.pkg.dev/cloudrun/container/hello \
  --region=europe-west1 --service-account=$SA
takeaways: Attach service accounts to resources instead of using key files
One minimal service account per workload
serviceAccountUser on the SA controls who can run code as it
pitfalls: Downloading a JSON key to test locally and committing it to Git.
Leaving workloads on the default compute service account with broad roles.

quiz.q: Bob can deploy Cloud Run services but gets a permission error when setting --service-account=admin-sa. What is missing?
quiz.explain: Attaching a service account requires permission to act as that specific account, which roles/iam.serviceAccountUser grants.

concepts.name: Compute Engine VMs
concepts.summary: Create, connect to and manage virtual machines: machine types, images, disks, SSH and cheap Spot VMs.
concepts.why: VMs are the most flexible way to run software in Google Cloud, and the layer underneath GKE and many other services.
concepts.body:
**Compute Engine** is Google Cloud's VM service: you ask for a virtual machine in a zone, and within seconds you have a Linux (or Windows) computer you can SSH into, billed by the second.

When creating one you choose:
- **Machine type**: how many CPUs and how much memory. Names are family plus size: `e2-medium` is the cheap everyday default, `n4-standard-4` is general purpose with 4 CPUs, `c4-` machines are for heavy number-crunching, and `t2a-` machines use Arm processors.
- **Image**: the operating system the disk starts from, such as Debian or Ubuntu. Pick an **image family** (`debian-12`) and you always get its latest patched version.
- **Disks**: the disk the operating system starts from, plus optional extra **Persistent Disk** or Hyperdisk volumes — network-attached disks that can outlive the VM unless you set them to be deleted with it.
- **Identity and network**: which service account the VM acts as, which network it joins, and whether it gets an **external IP address** — the public number other computers on the internet use to reach it.

Connect with `gcloud compute ssh web-1`. It creates an SSH key pair, puts the public key on the VM and logs you in. Add `--tunnel-through-iap` and the connection goes through Google's **Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP)**, a Google service that checks your identity and forwards you in, so you can reach VMs that have no external IP at all.

A **startup script** runs every time the VM starts: put a shell script in the VM's settings under the key `startup-script` — handy for simple setup such as installing nginx. A stopped VM no longer pays for CPU and memory, but its disks and any reserved static IP address are still charged.

**Spot VMs** (`--provisioning-model=SPOT`) are Google's spare capacity at a large discount, but Google can take them back at any moment with 30 seconds' warning. They're great for work that can be split up and retried, like converting a big pile of videos overnight — never for a single server whose data you can't afford to lose.
concepts.code:
gcloud compute instances create web-1 \
  --zone=europe-west1-b --machine-type=e2-medium \
  --image-family=debian-12 --image-project=debian-cloud \
  --tags=http-server --metadata=startup-script='#!/bin/bash
apt-get update && apt-get install -y nginx'

# List VMs with their zone, state and external IP
gcloud compute instances list --format="table(name,zone.basename(),status,networkInterfaces[0].accessConfigs[0].natIP)"
# NAME   ZONE            STATUS   NAT_IP
# web-1  europe-west1-b  RUNNING  34.76.12.34

gcloud compute ssh web-1 --zone=europe-west1-b   # SSH keys handled for you
gcloud compute instances stop web-1 --zone=europe-west1-b
takeaways: Pick the machine family by workload; e2 is the cheap default
Use image families to always get the latest patched image
Stopped VMs still pay for disks and static IPs
Spot VMs are cheap but can be taken back at any time
pitfalls: Keeping a database on a Spot VM, or on a local SSD (a fast disk inside the physical machine that is wiped when the VM stops), and losing the data when the VM goes away.

quiz.q: You stop a VM for the weekend. What are you still billed for?
options: Its persistent disks (and any reserved static IP)
quiz.explain: Charges for CPU and memory stop, but disks and reserved addresses keep costing money.

concepts.name: VPC networks and subnets
concepts.summary: Your private network in Google Cloud: global VPC networks, regional subnets, internal and external IP addresses, and routes.
concepts.why: Every VM and private database gets its address from a VPC subnet, and that layout is hard to change later.
concepts.body:
Computers find each other by **IP address**, a number like `10.10.0.5`, much like a street address. A **VPC network** (virtual private cloud) is your own private network inside Google Cloud: machines on it get addresses that only other machines on that network can reach, like extension numbers on an office phone system.

In Google Cloud a VPC network is **global**: one network spans every region, so a VM in Belgium and one in Iowa can talk over private addresses with no extra setup. The network is divided into **subnets**, and each subnet is **regional**: it belongs to one region and owns one range of addresses.

Ranges are written in **CIDR** notation, like `10.10.0.0/20`. The number after the slash says how many leading bits of the address are fixed; the rest are free. `/20` leaves 12 bits free, about 4,000 addresses, and a smaller number means a bigger range. Addresses starting with `10.` are reserved for private networks and never used on the public internet.

Two ways to create a network:
- **Auto mode** creates one subnet in every region from a fixed block, `10.128.0.0/9`. The `default` network in every new project is auto mode, with firewall rules (filters that decide which traffic may reach a VM) that let a lot in. Fine for experiments only.
- **Custom mode** creates no subnets; you add exactly the ranges you planned. Use it for anything real, so your ranges don't clash with your office network or other VPCs you may connect later.

Each VM gets an **internal IP address** from its subnet. An **external IP address**, reachable from the internet, is optional; a static one is reserved and kept, an ephemeral one changes when the VM stops. VMs without an external IP can still reach the internet through Cloud NAT and reach Google's own services through Private Google Access (both covered later).

**Routes** tell the network where to send traffic for each range of addresses, like signposts at a junction. Every network gets automatic routes to its own subnets and a default route, `0.0.0.0/0` (meaning "any address"), out to the internet. You add your own routes when you connect other networks, such as your office over a **VPN**, an encrypted tunnel across the internet.

Several VPC networks in one project are cut off from each other unless you connect them (covered later).
concepts.code:
# Custom mode: no subnets until you add them
gcloud compute networks create shop-vpc --subnet-mode=custom

gcloud compute networks subnets create shop-euw1 --network=shop-vpc \
  --region=europe-west1 --range=10.10.0.0/20

gcloud compute networks subnets create shop-use1 --network=shop-vpc \
  --region=us-east1 --range=10.20.0.0/20

gcloud compute networks subnets list --network=shop-vpc
# NAME       REGION        NETWORK   RANGE
# shop-euw1  europe-west1  shop-vpc  10.10.0.0/20
# shop-use1  us-east1      shop-vpc  10.20.0.0/20

# Where does traffic for each range go next?
gcloud compute routes list --filter="network:shop-vpc" --format="value(destRange,nextHopGateway.basename())"
takeaways: VPC networks and routes are global; subnets are regional
Use custom mode and plan ranges that don't overlap
External IPs are optional; private VMs reach out through Cloud NAT
pitfalls: Building production on the auto-mode default network, whose ranges are the same in every project, so two such networks can never be connected later.

quiz.q: A VM in us-east1 and one in europe-west1 are in the same VPC. What do they need to talk over internal IPs?
options: Nothing beyond firewall rules allowing it
quiz.explain: A VPC network is global, so subnets in different regions can already reach each other; only firewall rules apply.

concepts.name: Firewall rules
concepts.summary: Firewall rules decide which network traffic may reach your VMs: priorities, the built-in rules, and targeting by tag or service account.
concepts.why: Firewall rules are the main network guard for VMs, and most 'cannot connect' problems end here.
concepts.body:
A **firewall** is a filter that decides which network traffic may pass — like a guard at a building's door checking a list. In a VPC network, **firewall rules** are that list, and they are checked at every VM.

Each rule has a direction (`INGRESS` for incoming traffic, `EGRESS` for outgoing), an action (allow or deny), the **protocol** and ports it covers, a source or destination address range, a **target** (which VMs it applies to) and a **priority** from 0 to 65535 — the lower number wins. A protocol is the set of rules a kind of traffic follows; SSH and the web use one called **TCP**, so `tcp:22` means SSH connections.

Rules are **stateful**: when a connection is allowed in one direction, the replies coming back are allowed automatically. You write a rule for the visitor coming in; you don't need a second rule for your VM's answer.

Every VPC network also has two **implied rules** at the lowest priority: deny all incoming traffic and allow all outgoing. So a new custom-mode network accepts nothing from outside until you add rules.

Targets decide which VMs a rule applies to:
- all VMs in the network;
- VMs carrying a **network tag**, a short word such as `http-server` that you put on the VM;
- VMs running as a given **service account**, which is stronger, because changing a VM's service account needs more permission than editing its tags.

Two source ranges are worth knowing. `35.235.240.0/20` is where Identity-Aware Proxy connections come from, so allowing SSH from it lets `gcloud compute ssh --tunnel-through-iap` reach VMs without an external IP. `130.211.0.0/22` and `35.191.0.0/16` are where Google's load balancers send their **health checks**, small automatic tests that confirm each VM is working. (A **load balancer** spreads visitors across many VMs; it gets its own lesson.)

Larger companies also use **firewall policies** set on a folder or the whole organization, so a security team can enforce rules across many networks; these are checked before a network's own rules. When you're stuck on a "can't connect" problem, turn on **firewall rules logging** for a rule to see exactly what it allowed or denied.
concepts.code:
# SSH only through IAP, only to VMs tagged ssh
gcloud compute firewall-rules create shop-allow-iap-ssh --network=shop-vpc \
  --direction=INGRESS --action=ALLOW --rules=tcp:22 \
  --source-ranges=35.235.240.0/20 --target-tags=ssh

# Web traffic (ports 80 and 443) from anywhere, to VMs running as the web service account
gcloud compute firewall-rules create shop-allow-http --network=shop-vpc \
  --direction=INGRESS --action=ALLOW --rules=tcp:80,tcp:443 \
  --source-ranges=0.0.0.0/0 \
  --target-service-accounts=web@shop-dev-4821.iam.gserviceaccount.com

# Then connect without an external IP
gcloud compute ssh web-1 --zone=europe-west1-b --tunnel-through-iap
takeaways: Rules are stateful; replies are allowed automatically
Built-in rules: deny all incoming, allow all outgoing
The lower priority number wins
Target by service account for stronger control than tags
pitfalls: Opening tcp:22 (SSH) to 0.0.0.0/0 — the whole internet — instead of only IAP's range.

quiz.q: Two ingress rules match an incoming connection: allow at priority 1000 and deny at priority 900. What happens?
options: Both are logged and the connection waits
Denied, because 900 is the higher priority
quiz.explain: Lower numbers are higher priority, so the deny at 900 is evaluated first and applies.

concepts.name: Cloud Storage buckets and objects
concepts.summary: Store files as objects in buckets: create buckets, copy files in and out with gcloud storage, and control who can read them.
concepts.why: Cloud Storage holds everything from user uploads and backups to raw data files and static websites.
concepts.body:
**Cloud Storage** is Google's file storage service: practically unlimited, and you pay only for what you keep. It is **object storage**: each file is an **object** — its bytes plus a little information about it, its **metadata** (size, type, upload time) — and objects live in **buckets**, the top-level containers.

Bucket names are unique across all of Google Cloud, like website names (one could be `shop-dev-4821-uploads`). A bucket has a **location** — a region, a pair of regions or a multi-region — chosen when you create it and never changed.

There are no real directories: `reports/2026/q3.csv` is one object whose name happens to contain slashes, and tools show the parts before each `/` as folders. (Buckets created with the optional **hierarchical namespace** do have real folders, which helps big data-processing jobs.)

Use the `gcloud storage` commands (`cp`, `ls`, `rm`, `rsync`); they replace the older `gsutil` tool and are faster for big transfers.

Who may read and write is decided by IAM. Three settings to know:
- **Uniform bucket-level access** makes IAM the only access check, instead of also letting each object carry its own old-style permission list. Turn it on; it is the recommended setting.
- **Public access prevention** blocks granting anything to `allUsers`, so nothing can be made public by accident. Many organizations enforce it.
- To share one file for a while, create a **signed URL**: a link with a built-in expiry time that works without signing in, instead of making anything public.

An upload always replaces the whole object; you can't change part of one. After an upload succeeds, every read and listing sees the new version straight away. Deleted objects are kept for a **soft delete** period (7 days by default) and can be restored — and you pay to store them meanwhile.

A single object can be up to 5 TiB (about 5,500 GB), and `gcloud storage` splits big files into pieces and uploads them in parallel automatically.
concepts.code:
gcloud storage buckets create gs://shop-dev-4821-uploads \
  --location=europe-west1 --uniform-bucket-level-access --public-access-prevention

gcloud storage cp ./report.csv gs://shop-dev-4821-uploads/reports/2026/
gcloud storage ls gs://shop-dev-4821-uploads/reports/
# gs://shop-dev-4821-uploads/reports/2026/

gcloud storage cat gs://shop-dev-4821-uploads/reports/2026/report.csv | head -2
gcloud storage rsync ./site gs://shop-dev-4821-uploads/site --recursive

# Link that works for 1 hour, without making anything public
# (signed by a service account you are allowed to act as)
gcloud storage sign-url gs://shop-dev-4821-uploads/reports/2026/report.csv --duration=1h \
  --impersonate-service-account=signer@shop-dev-4821.iam.gserviceaccount.com
takeaways: Buckets have a fixed location and a globally unique name
Folders are just parts of object names
Use uniform bucket-level access and IAM; share with signed URLs
Prefer gcloud storage over gsutil
pitfalls: Granting allUsers the objectViewer role on a whole bucket just to share one file.

quiz.q: How do you rename a 'folder' holding 10,000 objects in a bucket without hierarchical namespace?
options: Copy every object to its new name and delete the old ones
Folders cannot contain that many objects
quiz.explain: Without hierarchical namespace, folders are only parts of object names, so a rename copies each object to its new name.

concepts.name: Cloud Run services
concepts.summary: Run a container as a web service with its own HTTPS address that adds copies as traffic grows and shrinks to zero when idle.
concepts.why: Cloud Run is the quickest path from a container to a live web address, with no servers to look after.
concepts.body:
When you open a website, your browser sends a **request** — "give me this page" — to a server, and the server sends back a **response**. The rules for that exchange are called **HTTP**; **HTTPS** is the same thing scrambled so that nobody in between can read it. Every page or service has a **URL**, a web address such as `https://shop.example.com/orders`.

**Cloud Run** runs your container as such a web service. You give it a container image; it gives you an HTTPS URL. It starts copies of your container (**instances**) when requests arrive, adds more as traffic grows (**autoscaling**), and stops them all when nobody is calling, so an idle service costs nothing.

Your container has to follow a simple contract:
- Listen for HTTP requests on the port given in the `PORT` environment variable (8080 by default).
- Be **stateless**: keep nothing you need later on local disk or in memory. Files written inside the container live in memory and vanish when that instance stops, and the next request may go to a different instance. Keep data in a database or Cloud Storage instead.

Each deploy creates a new **revision**: a fixed, unchangeable snapshot of your image and settings. You can send a small share of traffic to a new revision to try it safely — a **canary** — and switch back to the previous revision instantly if something breaks.

Settings that matter:
- **Concurrency**: how many requests one instance handles at the same time (default 80). Lower it for CPU-heavy work.
- **Min and max instances**: with zero instances running, the first request waits a second or two while one starts — a **cold start**. `--min-instances=1` keeps one ready; `--max-instances` caps cost and protects your database from too many connections.
- **CPU, memory** and the request **timeout**, how long one request may take before it is cut off (default 5 minutes, up to 60).
- **Who may call it**: by default callers must sign in and hold `roles/run.invoker`; `--allow-unauthenticated` makes the service public.
- **Service account**: the identity your code runs as.

`gcloud run deploy --source .` even builds the image for you, using Cloud Build (Google's build service) and storing the result in Artifact Registry (its image registry). For work that runs to completion instead of answering requests — a nightly report, say — use **Cloud Run jobs**.
concepts.code:
# Dockerfile next to app.py:  FROM python:3.13-slim ... CMD exec gunicorn -b :$PORT app:app
gcloud run deploy orders-api --source . --region=europe-west1 \
  --service-account=orders-api@shop-dev-4821.iam.gserviceaccount.com \
  --allow-unauthenticated --min-instances=0 --max-instances=20 --concurrency=40
# Service URL: https://orders-api-987654321098.europe-west1.run.app

# Canary: send 10% of traffic to the newest revision
gcloud run services update-traffic orders-api --region=europe-west1 \
  --to-revisions=orders-api-00007-xyz=10,orders-api-00006-abc=90

gcloud run services logs read orders-api --region=europe-west1 --limit=20
takeaways: Listen on $PORT and keep instances stateless
Every deploy is a revision; split traffic to try new ones safely
Tune concurrency, min and max instances
Services need signed-in callers unless you allow unauthenticated access
pitfalls: Doing background work after sending the response: by default Cloud Run gives an instance CPU only while it is handling a request, so that work crawls or stalls.

quiz.q: Right after deploy, your Cloud Run service answers browsers with '403 Forbidden' (access refused). Most likely cause?
options: The container is not listening on $PORT
The service only accepts signed-in callers, and allUsers lacks roles/run.invoker
The region does not support HTTPS
quiz.explain: Services require callers to sign in by default; a public service needs --allow-unauthenticated so allUsers gets roles/run.invoker.

concepts.name: Authentication: ADC and impersonation
concepts.summary: How Google's client libraries find credentials (Application Default Credentials), and how to run local code as a service account without keys.
concepts.why: The same code must sign in on your laptop, in automated build pipelines and in production, without passwords or keys written into it.
concepts.body:
When your own code talks to Google Cloud — say a Python script that lists buckets — it usually goes through a **client library**: a package Google publishes for each language (`google-cloud-storage` for Python, for example) that wraps the API in ordinary functions. Before calling anything, the library needs **credentials**, the proof of who is calling.

Client libraries find credentials through **Application Default Credentials (ADC)**, which looks in this order:
- the file named by the `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` environment variable;
- the file written by `gcloud auth application-default login`, which holds your own login, in your gcloud settings directory;
- the **metadata server**, present on Compute Engine, GKE, Cloud Run, Cloud Run functions and Cloud Build, which hands out tokens for the attached service account.

So code written as `storage.Client()` works everywhere unchanged: on your laptop it uses your ADC login, in production the attached service account. Note that `gcloud auth login` (signs in the gcloud tool) and `gcloud auth application-default login` (signs in your code) are separate logins stored in separate places.

To test with exactly production's permissions, **impersonate** the service account instead of downloading a key: Google gives you short-lived tokens for that account, after checking that you hold `roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator` on it. Then:

```bash
gcloud auth application-default login --impersonate-service-account=orders-api@shop-dev-4821.iam.gserviceaccount.com
```

gcloud has the same feature per command (`--impersonate-service-account`) or as a saved property (`auth/impersonate_service_account`).

With your personal login, some APIs also want to know which project to count the usage against — the **quota project**. If you see a warning about it, `gcloud auth application-default set-quota-project PROJECT_ID` fixes it.
concepts.code:
# pip install google-cloud-storage
import google.auth
from google.cloud import storage

credentials, project = google.auth.default()
print(type(credentials).__name__, project)
# laptop with ADC login:      Credentials shop-dev-4821
# Cloud Run / GCE / GKE:      Credentials (compute_engine) shop-dev-4821

client = storage.Client()          # same discovery, no key file
for bucket in client.list_buckets(max_results=3):
    print(bucket.name)
takeaways: ADC order: GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS, gcloud ADC file, metadata server
gcloud auth login is for the CLI; application-default login is for your code
Impersonate a service account (Token Creator) instead of using keys
pitfalls: Leaving GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS pointing at an old key file, which silently takes priority over everything else.

quiz.q: Your code works in Cloud Run but locally fails with 'default credentials not found' even though gcloud commands work. Why?
options: You ran gcloud auth login but not gcloud auth application-default login
Client libraries require a JSON key
quiz.explain: gcloud's own login and ADC are stored separately; client libraries only read ADC.

concepts.name: Managed instance groups and autoscaling
concepts.summary: Run many identical VMs from an instance template, with autoscaling, automatic repair and gradual rolling updates.
concepts.why: A single VM is one point of failure; a managed group repairs itself, grows with traffic and is what load balancers send traffic to.
concepts.body:
Compute Engine calls each VM an **instance**. Instead of creating VMs one by one, you can describe one VM once and let Google keep a whole group of copies running.

An **instance template** is that description: machine type, image, disks, startup script, network tags, service account. Templates are **immutable** — once created they can't be edited. A **managed instance group (MIG)** creates and looks after N identical VMs from one template.

What a MIG does for you:
- **Autoscaling**: adds VMs when they get busy and removes them when they're idle, between a minimum and maximum size. "Busy" can mean CPU use, load balancer traffic, a Cloud Monitoring measurement or a schedule.
- **Autohealing**: with a health check attached, a VM that stops answering is deleted and recreated. Set an initial delay long enough for the VM to start and your app to come up.
- **Regional MIGs** spread VMs across the zones of a region, so a zone outage doesn't take the service down. Prefer them over zonal MIGs for anything serving users.
- **Rolling updates**: point the group at a new template and it replaces VMs a few at a time, controlled by `--max-surge` (extra VMs allowed during the update) and `--max-unavailable` (VMs allowed to be down).

Because templates can't change, a change means a new template (`web-tpl-v2`) plus a rolling update. You can also update only a fraction of VMs first, as a canary.

Any VM in a MIG may be deleted and recreated at any time, so the VMs must be **stateless** — keeping nothing on their own disks that you'd miss — and must set themselves up when they start, from a startup script, a ready-made image, or containers.

MIGs are the usual thing a load balancer sends traffic to (its **backend**). Unmanaged instance groups also exist, but they only group VMs you already have and do none of the above.
concepts.code:
gcloud compute instance-templates create web-tpl-v1 \
  --machine-type=e2-small --image-family=debian-12 --image-project=debian-cloud \
  --tags=http-server --metadata-from-file=startup-script=startup.sh

# Health check: request /healthz on port 80 and expect a success reply
gcloud compute health-checks create http web-hc --port=80 --request-path=/healthz

gcloud compute instance-groups managed create web-mig --region=europe-west1 \
  --template=web-tpl-v1 --size=2 --health-check=web-hc --initial-delay=120

gcloud compute instance-groups managed set-autoscaling web-mig --region=europe-west1 \
  --min-num-replicas=2 --max-num-replicas=10 --target-cpu-utilization=0.6

# Later: roll out a new template with no loss of capacity
gcloud compute instance-groups managed rolling-action start-update web-mig \
  --region=europe-west1 --version=template=web-tpl-v2 --max-surge=3 --max-unavailable=0
takeaways: Templates can't be edited; a change = new template + rolling update
Regional MIGs survive a zone outage
Autohealing needs a health check and an initial delay longer than start-up time
pitfalls: Setting the autohealing initial delay shorter than the VM's start-up time, so VMs are recreated in an endless loop.

quiz.q: How do you change the machine type of every VM in a MIG?
options: Edit the instance template in place
SSH into each VM and resize it
Delete the MIG; resizing is impossible
Create a new template and start a rolling update
quiz.explain: Templates cannot be edited; the MIG rolls VMs over to a new template.

concepts.name: Storage classes, lifecycle and versioning
concepts.summary: Match the storage class to how often data is read, automate moves and deletion with lifecycle rules, and protect data with versioning.
concepts.why: Storage bills grow quietly; lifecycle rules and the right storage class can cut them tenfold.
concepts.body:
Every object has a **storage class**. All classes answer just as fast and keep your data equally safe; they differ in price per GB stored, a fee per GB read (the **retrieval fee**) and a **minimum storage duration**:
- **Standard**: data read often; no minimum.
- **Nearline**: read about once a month; 30-day minimum.
- **Coldline**: read about once a quarter; 90-day minimum.
- **Archive**: read less than once a year; 365-day minimum.

Deleting or replacing an object before its minimum is billed as if it had stayed the full time. And retrieval fees make the colder classes expensive if you read from them often.

**Lifecycle rules** act on objects automatically: change the storage class after N days, delete after N days, delete old versions, or clean up uploads that were started but never finished. Google checks the rules in the background, usually within a day of an object qualifying — not instantly. If you can't predict how data will be used, **Autoclass** moves each object between classes based on how it is actually read.

**Object versioning** keeps the previous copy as a *noncurrent version* whenever an object is overwritten or deleted, so you can get it back. Pair it with a lifecycle rule that deletes old versions, or your costs grow forever.

For legal record-keeping there are **retention policies** (objects can't be deleted before a given age; the policy can even be locked permanently) and **object holds**, which freeze single objects. Separately, soft delete protects against accidental deletes even without versioning.
concepts.code:
cat > lifecycle.json <<'EOF'
{"rule": [
  {"action": {"type": "SetStorageClass", "storageClass": "NEARLINE"},
   "condition": {"age": 30, "matchesStorageClass": ["STANDARD"]}},
  {"action": {"type": "SetStorageClass", "storageClass": "ARCHIVE"},
   "condition": {"age": 365}},
  {"action": {"type": "Delete"},
   "condition": {"isLive": false, "numNewerVersions": 3}}
]}
EOF
# The third rule deletes old versions once 3 newer ones exist
gcloud storage buckets update gs://shop-dev-4821-uploads \
  --lifecycle-file=lifecycle.json --versioning
gcloud storage buckets describe gs://shop-dev-4821-uploads --format="yaml(lifecycle_config,versioning_enabled)"
takeaways: Every class answers equally fast; colder = cheaper to store, pricier to read, longer minimums
Lifecycle rules automate class changes and deletion
Versioning needs a cleanup rule for old versions
pitfalls: Moving often-read data to Coldline to save money, then paying more in retrieval fees.

quiz.q: You upload an object to Archive and delete it after 10 days. How long are you billed for?
quiz.explain: Archive has a 365-day minimum storage duration, charged on early deletion.

concepts.name: Cloud SQL
concepts.summary: Managed PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server: editions, high availability, backups and safe ways to connect.
concepts.why: It is the default home for an app's relational database on Google Cloud.
concepts.body:
Most apps keep their data in a **relational database**: tables of rows and columns, like linked spreadsheets, that you read and change with **SQL**, a language for asking questions such as `SELECT name FROM customers`. PostgreSQL and MySQL are the popular free ones.

**Cloud SQL** runs PostgreSQL, MySQL or SQL Server for you. Google sets up the machine, installs updates, takes backups, and keeps copies (**replicas**) ready to take over. You still own the **schema** (which tables and columns exist), your queries, and choosing a big enough machine.

Key choices at creation:
- **Edition**: Enterprise, or Enterprise Plus with faster machines, a memory cache for reads, near-zero-downtime maintenance and a higher uptime promise.
- **Machine shape**: CPUs and memory, plus SSD storage that can grow automatically.
- **Availability type**: `ZONAL`, or `REGIONAL` for **high availability** — a standby copy in another zone that receives every write at the same moment, and takes over automatically if the main one fails (**failover**).
- **Connectivity**: an internal (private) IP address inside your VPC network, a public IP, or both.

Backups: automated daily backups, plus **point-in-time recovery** — restoring the database as it was at any second, rebuilt from its log of changes. **Read replicas**, in the same or another region, take reading load off the main database and can stand in after a disaster. The high-availability standby can't be read from; it only waits.

Connecting safely: never open a public IP to `0.0.0.0/0`. Use the private IP, or the **Cloud SQL Auth Proxy** (a small program that runs next to your app) or Google's language connectors. They check your identity with IAM and encrypt the traffic without you handling certificates. Cloud Run has this built in: `--add-cloudsql-instances` gives your container a local connection file at `/cloudsql/PROJECT:REGION:INSTANCE`. **IAM database authentication** even lets users and service accounts log in without database passwords.

When a single database server is no longer big enough, look at AlloyDB or Spanner (covered in the database-choices lesson).
concepts.code:
gcloud sql instances create shop-pg --database-version=POSTGRES_17 \
  --edition=ENTERPRISE --cpu=2 --memory=8GiB --region=europe-west1 \
  --availability-type=REGIONAL --enable-point-in-time-recovery
gcloud sql databases create shop --instance=shop-pg
gcloud sql users create app --instance=shop-pg --password="$(openssl rand -base64 24)"

# Local development through the Auth Proxy (uses your ADC credentials)
cloud-sql-proxy shop-dev-4821:europe-west1:shop-pg --port 5432 &
psql "host=127.0.0.1 port=5432 dbname=shop user=app"

# Cloud Run: connection file at /cloudsql/shop-dev-4821:europe-west1:shop-pg
gcloud run deploy orders-api --image=IMAGE --region=europe-west1 \
  --add-cloudsql-instances=shop-dev-4821:europe-west1:shop-pg
takeaways: REGIONAL availability = standby in another zone with automatic failover
Turn on point-in-time recovery; add read replicas for reading load and disaster recovery
Connect via private IP or the Auth Proxy/connectors, never a public IP open to everyone
pitfalls: Expecting the high-availability standby to serve reads; use a read replica for that.
